title: Ginger for Arthritis: Evidence and Safety
meta_title: Ginger for Arthritis: Evidence and Safety
meta_description: Ginger supplements and arthritis: uncertain benefits, possible side effects, medicine checks and what NICE does and does not recommend.
excerpt: Ginger is a popular kitchen remedy for joint pain. Trials in osteoarthritis suggest a small benefit at best, and the evidence is of moderate to poor quality. This guide explains what the research shows, real safety points including blood thinners, ginger for medicine-related nausea, and simple ways to enjoy ginger as food.

content:
Ginger supplements have been studied for knee osteoarthritis, but the results do not establish a reliable benefit for every person or product. Research on extracts cannot tell us that ginger tea or a ginger shot treats arthritis. Do not replace prescribed treatment with ginger.

What does the research tell us?

The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says ginger supplements might help knee osteoarthritis symptoms, while noting that much of the research is poor quality. Its February 2025 summary says applying ginger to the skin has not been shown to help knee osteoarthritis.

A 2025 review comparing nutritional supplements illustrates why a simple promise would be misleading. Ginger was associated with improvement on one pain scale, but its results were not statistically significant for WOMAC pain, stiffness or function. Preparations, doses and follow-up varied. These findings do not identify a particular shop product, a standard dose or lasting benefit.

A 2026 review of seven trials also describes possible symptom benefit, but calls for more work on dosing, long-term effects and safety. This does not settle which preparation, if any, would be suitable for an individual.

Laboratory explanations of inflammation are not proof that a supplement improves everyday pain or prevents joint damage. This guide does not use them to recommend ginger, rank it against ibuprofen or promise a result after a set number of weeks.

Where does NICE guidance fit?

NICE osteoarthritis guidance identifies tailored exercise and weight management, when appropriate, alongside information and support as core care. It is not an endorsement of ginger. If pain limits activity, ask your clinician about adapting exercise and reviewing pain relief.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE says complementary therapies must not replace conventional treatment, and evidence for long-term benefit is limited or absent. A food or supplement is not a substitute for disease-modifying treatment.

Food and concentrated supplements are different

Using ginger for flavour in a meal is not the same as taking an extract capsule. The trials do not establish an arthritis-treatment dose for ginger tea, fresh ginger or shots. This guide does not prescribe a supplement dose or suggest a two-to-three-month self-trial.

If hand pain makes food preparation difficult, ready-prepared ginger can be an option for flavour. You do not need to buy a supplement to include ginger in cooking. Check the ingredients of sweetened drinks and foods rather than assuming their name makes them a treatment.

What should you check for safety?

NCCIH lists abdominal discomfort, heartburn, diarrhoea and mouth or throat irritation as possible effects of oral ginger. It advises speaking with a healthcare professional before using herbal products if you take medicines. Ask before using ginger supplements during pregnancy; little is known about safety while breastfeeding.

If you take warfarin, check new herbal products with your prescriber or anticoagulant team. NHS warfarin guidance warns that medicines, herbal remedies and supplements can affect treatment. This is a reason to check the exact product, not proof that all ginger preparations have the same interaction.

For methotrexate, the NHS says there is not enough information to establish the safety of other herbal remedies and supplements alongside it. Ask your rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting one. Do not change methotrexate or folic acid yourself.

When should you get help?

Tell your healthcare team if nausea, reflux or poor appetite affects eating. Do not change medicine timing or dose to accommodate a supplement without advice.

Vomiting blood always needs medical help. Call 999 or go to A&E if it occurs with feeling unwell, faintness, confusion, breathing changes, cold clammy skin, tummy pain or black stools. If it has stopped and there are no other symptoms, get urgent GP advice or 111. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

A suddenly very painful or hot, swollen joint needs urgent assessment, even without fever. In England, Scotland and Wales, contact an urgent GP service or 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. See NHS septic arthritis advice. Do not wait for a supplement to help.

General information, not a personal supplement recommendation. Follow your own healthcare team's advice. An editorial revision does not imply an independent clinical review.
